This prolonged binding of myosin to actin increases force generation, but slows actin motility, decreases cyclical muscle power generation and reduces flight ability.

claim: In the post-power stroke state, the N-terminus and R146 are distant from the lever arm.

claim: Drosophila, scallop and human β-cardiac myosins show strong sequence similarity in the R146 region.

claim: R146 displays charge interaction with E775 with a contact distance of 3.0 Å in the pre-power stroke state.

claim: The close contact distances between R146 and E774/E775 permit the formation of salt bridges.
source: The close contact distances permit the formation of salt bridges between the positively charged R146 and the negatively charged E774 and E775 residues.

claim: Three independent transgenic inserts (PwMhcR146N-11, PwMhcR146N-15, PwMhcR146N-28) were obtained that mapped to the third chromosome.

claim: RT-PCR verified that each transgenic line expresses only the mutant myosin in the IFM.
source: RT-PCR of RNA isolated from dissected IFM verified that each transgenic line expresses only the mutant myosin in the IFM and that the normal alternative exon splicing pattern is not disrupted (see Materials and methods).

claim: The normal alternative exon splicing pattern is not disrupted in the transgenic lines.
source: RT-PCR of RNA isolated from dissected IFM verified that each transgenic line expresses only the mutant myosin in the IFM and that the normal alternative exon splicing pattern is not disrupted (see Materials and methods).
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR analysis performed in this study.

claim: Upper thoraces of mutant 2-day-old adult female flies from lines 11, 15 and 28 express normalized ratios of myosin to actin that are essentially identical to the wild-type control transgenic line PwMhc2.
source: SDS-PAGE analysis confirmed that upper thoraces of mutant 2-day-old adult female flies from lines 11, 15 and 28 express normalized ratios of myosin to actin (1.06 ± 0.06, 0.99 ± 0.02, 0.98 ± 0.01, respectively) that are essentially identical to the wild-type control transgenic line PwMhc2 (1.00 ± 0.04).
evidence: Supported by SDS-PAGE analysis performed in this study.

claim: Ca-ATPase rate of R146N myosin (16.64 ± 1.87 sec−1) increased significantly, about two-fold compared to wild-type myosin (9.51 ± 1.08 sec−1).
source: Both Ca-ATPase (16.64 ± 1.87 vs. 9.51 ± 1.08 sec−1) and basal Mg-ATPase (0.62 ± 0.14 vs. 0.25 ± 0.04 sec−1) rates of R146N myosin increased significantly, about two-fold compared to wild-type myosin (Figure 2A,B).

claim: Basal Mg-ATPase rate of R146N myosin (0.62 ± 0.14 sec−1) increased significantly, about two-fold compared to wild-type myosin (0.25 ± 0.04 sec−1).
source: Both Ca-ATPase (16.64 ± 1.87 vs. 9.51 ± 1.08 sec−1) and basal Mg-ATPase (0.62 ± 0.14 vs. 0.25 ± 0.04 sec−1) rates of R146N myosin increased significantly, about two-fold compared to wild-type myosin (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: Supported by ATPase assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Actin-stimulated Mg-ATPase activity (Vmax) of R146N myosin (1.57 ± 0.27 sec−1) was not significantly different from the control (1.62 ± 0.14 sec−1).
source: We found that actin-stimulated Mg-ATPase activity (Vmax) (Figure 2C) was not significantly different from the control (1.57 ± 0.27 vs. 1.62 ± 0.14 sec−1).
evidence: Supported by ATPase assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The Km of actin concentration relative to ATPase activity was significantly increased for R146N myosin (0.42 ± 0.06 µM) compared to control (0.31 ± 0.04 µM), indicating that a 35% higher actin concentration is required to reach 50% Vmax.
source: The Km of actin concentration relative to ATPase activity was significantly increased, indicating that a 35% higher actin concentration is required to reach 50% Vmax (0.42 ± 0.06 vs. 0.31 ± 0.04 µM) (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by ATPase assay data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The catalytic efficiency (Vmax/Km) of R146N myosin (3.80 ± 0.60 sec−1/µM) was significantly lower than that of the control (5.34 ± 1.07 sec−1/µM).
source: Further, the mutant's catalytic efficiency (defined as Vmax/Km) was significantly lower than that of the control (3.80 ± 0.60 vs. 5.34 ± 1.07 sec−1/µM) (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by ATPase assay data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The mutant myosin possesses an approximately two-fold reduction in its ability to drive actin filament sliding (3.32 ± 0.21 µm/s) compared to myosin isolated from control IFM (6.71 ± 0.17 µm/s).
source: Analysis of in vitro actin-sliding velocity data showed that the mutant myosin possesses an ~two fold reduction in its ability to drive actin filament sliding compared to myosin isolated from control IFM (3.32 ± 0.21 vs. 6.71 ± 0.17 µm/s) (Figure 2F).

claim: Transverse and longitudinal sections of R146N late-stage pupae showed normal sarcomeres containing double hexagonal arrays of thick and thin filaments, which are indistinguishable from those of the PwMhc2 homozygous control line.

claim: Transverse and longitudinal sections of R146N 2-hr-old adults showed normal sarcomeres containing double hexagonal arrays of thick and thin filaments, which are indistinguishable from those of the PwMhc2 homozygous control line.

evidence: Supported by transmission electron microscopy images shown in Figure 3H.

claim: R146N mutant myosin is capable of contributing to the formation of normal myofibrillar structures that begin to deteriorate at 2 days into adulthood, presumably as a result of mechanical stress during use.

claim: Fibers from R146N/+ heterozygotes showed decreased IFM fiber power generation over the frequency range 40–100 Hz.

evidence: This is an interpretation of the work loop and power generation data.

claim: Abnormally high stresses on the myofilaments likely result in the disruption of sarcomere integrity that develops over time in the IFM expressing the mutant myosin.
source: These abnormally high stresses on the myofilaments likely result in the disruption of sarcomere integrity that develops over time in the IFM expressing the mutant myosin (Figure 3), as well as the reduced flight ability and WBF (Table 4).
evidence: Based on correlation between mechanical stress and structural degeneration observed in electron microscopy.

claim: While the hearts in the mutants did not show a change in heart period, suggesting no overall change in kinetics, this is in agreement with no change for fmax in IFM and for actin-activated ATPase.
source: While the hearts in the mutants did not show a change in heart period (suggesting no overall change in kinetics, in agreement with no change for fmax in IFM and for actin-activated ATPase), the heart spent a greater portion of each heart period in systole compared to the control (Figure 7).
evidence: Based on comparison of cardiac and muscle mechanics data.

claim: The heart spending a greater portion of each heart period in systole is consistent with prolonged contractions arising from increased myosin attachment kinetics and a decreased detachment rate.
source: This is consistent with prolonged contractions arising from increased myosin attachment kinetics and a decreased detachment rate.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the cardiac physiological data.

claim: An enhanced attachment rate would increase the rate of force generation, which may partially account for the restricted cardiac phenotype.
source: An enhanced attachment rate would also increase the rate of force generation, which may partially account for the restricted cardiac phenotype.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the cardiac phenotype.

claim: The reduced fractional shortening observed for the R146N/+ heart may correspond to its optimal pumping mode, mimicking the improved IFM fiber mechanical performance at shorter muscle length changes.
source: The reduced fractional shortening observed for the R146N/+ heart may correspond to its optimal pumping mode, mimicking the improved IFM fiber mechanical performance at shorter muscle length changes.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation connecting cardiac and muscle mechanics observations.

claim: The observed myofibrillar discontinuity in cardiomyocytes could be caused by the same mechanism as IFM degeneration, that is, excessive tension generation disrupting the integrity of the sarcomeric ultrastructure.
source: At the ultrastructural level, the observed myofibrillar discontinuity in cardiomyocytes (Figure 6) could be caused by the same mechanism as IFM degeneration, that is, excessive tension generation disrupting the integrity of the sarcomeric ultrastructure.
evidence: This is an interpretation connecting cardiac and skeletal muscle structural observations.

claim: Hypertrophy can occur in the conical chamber of the Drosophila heart as a result of abnormal receptor tyrosine kinase pathway signaling.
source: We did not detect hypertrophy of the cardiomyocytes in R146N/+ heterozygotes, although it has been shown that hypertrophy can occur in the conical chamber of the Drosophila heart as a result of abnormal receptor tyrosine kinase pathway signaling (Yu et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: There is significant variability in the presence and degree of hypertrophy detected in patients carrying the 146N mutation.
source: It is important to note, however, that there is significant variability in the presence and degree of hypertrophy detected in patients carrying the 146N mutation (personal communication from Jodie Ingles, Sydney Medical School), suggesting that interacting genes or environment may play a role in hypertrophy.
evidence: Based on personal communication cited in the manuscript.

claim: Interacting genes or environment may play a role in hypertrophy in patients with the 146N mutation.
source: It is important to note, however, that there is significant variability in the presence and degree of hypertrophy detected in patients carrying the 146N mutation (personal communication from Jodie Ingles, Sydney Medical School), suggesting that interacting genes or environment may play a role in hypertrophy.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the variability in patient phenotypes.

claim: Cross-bridges in the Drosophila heart bind to thin filaments via Ca2+-dependent and Ca2+-independent mechanisms during diastole.
source: Interestingly, our data suggest that cross-bridges in the Drosophila heart bind to thin filaments via Ca2+-dependent and Ca2+-independent mechanisms during diastole.
evidence: Based on calcium chelation and blebbistatin treatment experiments.

claim: Small amounts of diastolic Ca2+ promote contraction and yield slightly shortened cardiomyocytes at rest in both mutant and control lines.
source: Our results imply that small amounts of diastolic Ca2+ promote contraction and yield slightly shortened cardiomyocytes at rest in both mutant and control lines.
evidence: Based on interpretation of calcium chelation experiments.

claim: Based upon the greater diameter increase in R146N/+ hearts compared to control hearts upon calcium chelation, disruption of Ca2+-handling in the mutant appears likely.
source: However, based upon the greater diameter increase (greater tension drop) in R146N/+ hearts compared to control hearts upon extra- and intracellular Ca2+ chelation with EGTA/EGTA,AM (Figure 8B), disruption of Ca2+-handling in the mutant appears likely, which may promote the restricted cardiac tube phenotype.
evidence: Based on interpretation of calcium chelation experiments shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Perturbation of Ca2+-handling in R146N/+ mutant fly hearts, as is frequently observed in human cardiomyopathies, may result in excessive diastolic Ca2+ levels, yielding enhancement of cell shortening and elevated basal tone.
source: Therefore, it is possible that perturbation of Ca2+-handling in R146N/+ mutant fly hearts, as is frequently observed in human cardiomyopathies (Kranias and Bers, 2007), results in excessive diastolic Ca2+ levels, yielding enhancement of cell shortening and elevated basal tone.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citation to prior literature on human cardiomyopathies.

claim: The higher duty ratio of R146N myosin could indirectly enhance the Ca2+ sensitivity of the cross-bridges through thin filament activation.
source: Additionally, the higher duty ratio of R146N myosin could indirectly enhance the Ca2+ sensitivity of the cross-bridges through thin filament activation.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism based on known properties of thin filament activation.

claim: Full thin filament activation requires both Ca2+ binding to troponin and strong binding of cross-bridges.
source: Full thin filament activation requires both Ca2+ binding to troponin and strong binding of cross-bridges.
evidence: This is established knowledge about thin filament activation.

claim: A higher duty-ratio myosin will have a greater number of myosin molecules strongly bound at a lower Ca2+ concentration than a lower-duty-ratio myosin.
source: Thus, a higher duty-ratio myosin will have a greater number of myosin molecules strongly bound at a lower Ca2+ concentration than a lower-duty-ratio myosin.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the definition of duty ratio.

claim: Expression of the high-duty-ratio EMB myosin in the jump muscle caused enhanced Ca2+ sensitivity for tension development compared to jump muscle myosin.
source: We experimentally demonstrated this when we expressed the high-duty-ratio EMB myosin in the jump muscle, which caused enhanced Ca2+ sensitivity for tension development compared to jump muscle myosin (Eldred et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature from the authors' group.

claim: The same concentration of Ca2+ in the R146N/+ mutant heart would generate higher force than in the control, yielding decreased cardiac diameters.
source: Thus, the same concentration of Ca2+ in the R146N/+ mutant heart would generate higher force than in the control, yielding decreased cardiac diameters.
evidence: This is an inference based on the enhanced Ca2+ sensitivity mechanism.

claim: Blebbistatin impedes acto-myosin cycling.
source: Our analysis with blebbistatin, which impedes acto-myosin cycling (Kovács et al., 2004), indicates that a portion of the cross-bridges responsible for diastolic tone is calcium-independent in both control and R146N/+ hearts.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: A portion of the cross-bridges responsible for diastolic tone is calcium-independent in both control and R146N/+ hearts.
source: Our analysis with blebbistatin, which impedes acto-myosin cycling (Kovács et al., 2004), indicates that a portion of the cross-bridges responsible for diastolic tone is calcium-independent in both control and R146N/+ hearts.
evidence: Based on interpretation of blebbistatin treatment experiments.

claim: There is a greater diameter increase in R146N/+ hearts than in control hearts upon blebbistatin treatment, suggesting an enhanced number of Ca2+-independent cross-bridges.
source: Treatment with the drug (Figure 8C) shows that there is a greater diameter increase in R146N/+ hearts than in control hearts, suggesting an enhanced number of Ca2+-independent cross-bridges.
evidence: Based on interpretation of blebbistatin treatment experiments shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The enhancement of Ca2+-independent cross-bridges likely arises from the higher on-rate (actin affinity), which contributes to the restricted phenotype and impaired relaxation observed in R146N/+ mutant hearts.
source: This enhancement likely arises from the higher on-rate (actin affinity), which contributes to the restricted phenotype and impaired relaxation observed in R146N/+ mutant hearts.
evidence: This is an interpretation connecting the biochemical and physiological observations.

claim: Increased cross-bridge availability could result from disruption of the super-relaxed state that has been documented in both skeletal and cardiac muscles.
source: Increased cross-bridge availability could also result from disruption of the super-relaxed state that has been documented in both skeletal and cardiac muscles (Hooijman et al., 2011; Stewart et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The super-relaxed state correlates with the presence of the interacting head motif, wherein the dimeric heads of myosin molecules interact to reduce their actin binding and ATPase activity.
source: This state correlates with the presence of the interacting head motif, wherein the dimeric heads of myosin molecules interact to reduce their actin binding and ATPase activity (Trivedi et al., 2018; Woodhead et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Disruption of the interacting head motif by mutation is linked to myosin activation that correlates with HCM.
source: Disruption of this motif by mutation is linked to myosin activation that correlates with HCM (Alamo et al., 2017b; Nag et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Myosin is found in its pre-power stroke configuration in the interacting head motif.
source: Interestingly, myosin is found in its pre-power stroke configuration in the interacting head motif (Alamo et al., 2017a; Alamo et al., 2016) and disturbance of this state of filament packing by the R146N mutation could reduce the number of molecules in the super-relaxed state.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Disturbance of the interacting head motif by the R146N mutation could reduce the number of molecules in the super-relaxed state, which would enhance myosin activity within the myofibril, leading to the phenotypes observed.
source: Interestingly, myosin is found in its pre-power stroke configuration in the interacting head motif (Alamo et al., 2017a; Alamo et al., 2016) and disturbance of this state of filament packing by the R146N mutation could reduce the number of molecules in the super-relaxed state. This would enhance myosin activity within the myofibril, leading to the phenotypes we observed.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism connecting the molecular structure to the observed phenotypes.

claim: Drosophila myosins are capable of entering the interacting head motif.
source: Drosophila myosins are indeed capable of entering the interacting head motif (Lee et al., 2018), but the presence of the super-relaxed state in thick filaments or muscle fibers is yet to be documented.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The presence of the super-relaxed state in Drosophila thick filaments or muscle fibers is yet to be documented.
source: Drosophila myosins are indeed capable of entering the interacting head motif (Lee et al., 2018), but the presence of the super-relaxed state in thick filaments or muscle fibers is yet to be documented.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Enhancements in basal ATPase rate, length of systole and cross-bridge binding are concordant with expectations for a general mechanism of action for HCM mutations in humans.
source: In summary, our integrative analysis of the Drosophila analogue of the K146N human HCM mutation revealed increases in several, but not all, contractile parameters, as posited for a general mechanism of action for HCM mutations in humans (Spudich, 2014). Notably, enhancements in basal ATPase rate, length of systole and cross-bridge binding are concordant with these expectations.
evidence: Based on comparison of findings to expectations from cited literature.

claim: The restricted phenotype and reduced fractional shortening observed in the Drosophila heart mimic the diastolic dysfunction/impaired relaxation and reduced ejection fraction that can accompany HCM.
source: Further, the restricted phenotype and reduced fractional shortening observed in the Drosophila heart mimic the diastolic dysfunction/impaired relaxation and reduced ejection fraction that can accompany HCM (Davis et al., 2016; Maron, 2002; Maron and Maron, 2013; Masarone et al., 2018).
evidence: Based on comparison of findings to human HCM phenotypes described in cited literature.

claim: Restriction is a common phenotype produced in the Drosophila cardiac tube due to over-active cross-bridges.
source: The restricted phenotype observed in our model of an HCM mutant, as well as the restricted phenotypes arising from a hyperactive myosin (Cammarato et al., 2008) or mutant troponin T or actin that enhance myosin binding (Viswanathan et al., 2014; Viswanathan et al., 2017), suggest that restriction is a common phenotype produced in the Drosophila cardiac tube due to over-active cross-bridges.
evidence: Based on comparison of findings to prior studies cited.

claim: If all or most HCM mutations have increased force production as their basis, the restricted cardiac tube phenotype in Drosophila could serve as a useful screening tool for determining whether specific human mutations are causative of HCM.
source: If all or most HCM mutations have increased force production as their basis, the restricted cardiac tube phenotype in Drosophila could serve as a useful screening tool for determining whether specific human mutations are causative of HCM.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the findings of this study.

claim: The fly might serve to illuminate conserved signaling pathways that lead from contractile protein mutations to HCM.
source: The fly might also serve to illuminate conserved signaling pathways that lead from contractile protein mutations to HCM.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal for future research.

claim: The amelioration of the mutant phenotype through genetic or drug screens in Drosophila may yield insights into potential treatments for human HCM.
source: Further, the amelioration of the mutant phenotype through genetic or drug screens in Drosophila may yield insights into potential treatments for human HCM.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal for future research.
